india-f343399a92.headline: End Ukraine war, says Modi as he meets Putin during bilateral ahead of BRICS summit
india-f343399a92.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-f343399a92.fulltext:
Russian President Vladimir Putin, the first foreign dignitary to arrive in New Delhi for the BRICS Summit, held a bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday (September 11, 2026) and reviewed the full spectrum of bilateral ties. Mr. Modi reemphasized that “India stood ready to assist in peace efforts.”
“During today’s meeting we talked about: closer trade ties, including implementation of the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030. Cooperation in areas like infrastructure, energy, technology, defence, culture, and more,” said Prime Minister Modi in his remarks.
BRICS Summit 2026 updates on September 11
Sources said the two sides discussed steps to increase the bilateral trade target to $100 billion by 2030 and projects on civil nuclear cooperation. Mr. Modi reiterated his call to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict that has continued for more than four-and-a-half years.
“The two leaders reviewed progress in bilateral cooperation in political, economic, defence, energy, space, skill mobility, and people-to-people domains,” said the External Affairs Ministry after the meeting. The two leaders exchanged views on the conflict in West Asia and the spillover effects of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in the Black Sea region, affecting Indian seafarers. Several Indian sailors were killed in attacks by Russian and Ukrainian forces on foreign-flagged vessels.
“Prime Minister once again reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy was the way forward in resolving conflicts and India stood ready to assist in peace efforts,” the Ministry said in a press note. President Putin invited Prime Minister Modi for the 24th India-Russia Annual Summit, which India accepted. The dates of the summit will be decided as per “mutual convenience” following diplomatic consultations.
The talks featured ways to expand industrial cooperation with Russia, collaboration in railway and tunneling, developing a steel value chain, and more business-to-business opportunities. Russia has been increasing employment opportunities for Indian blue-collar professionals and cooperation in the mobility of skilled manpower.
Against the backdrop of the conflict in West Asia and supply chain disruptions, measures to ensure the flow of energy and fertilizers through strategic joint ventures were discussed, as was cooperation in critical minerals.
Prime Minister Modi gifted President Putin a Russian translation of Thirukkural,the classical Tamil poem collection authored by poet and philosopher Thiruvalluvar. Mr. Modi was accompanied by External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, National Security Adviser Ajit Doval, Principal Secretary Shaktikanta Das, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, and other senior officials in the meeting. The two leaders last met on the sidelines of the SCO summit in the Kyrgyz Republic’s capital, Bishkek, on August 31. Mr. Modi had called for an end to the Ukraine war then.
In a news release, the Kremlin said President Putin is expected to visit the INNOPROM exhibition organised jointly by the Indian and Russian Ministries of Commerce. He is scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with leaders of other countries during his stay in New Delhi. “The main agreements reached are expected to be reflected in the summit’s final document,” the Kremlin said.

ai-fad5f970d0.headline: Mecka AI nears $500M valuation in Sequoia-led deal amid rush for robot training data
ai-fad5f970d0.fulltext:
Mecka AI, a startup that collects and analyzes human motion data to train humanoid robots and other robotics, is nearing a new round led by Sequoia Capital at a valuation of about $500 million, according to two people with knowledge of the deal.
The new financing comes just three months after Mecka announced that it raised $60 million in a round led by Framework Ventures that included participation from Menlo Ventures, SV Angel, and Kindred Ventures.
TechCrunch has not learned the precise size of the new round. The terms of the deal are not final and could still change.
Mecka AI didn’t respond to a request for comment. Sequoia declined to comment.
Mecka AI was co-founded in 2024 by four entrepreneurs, including Canadians Josh Gao and Mogen Cheng, who previously built a restaurant fintech startup, and Jason Chong, who joined Coinbase after it acquired his crypto exchange. Duy Nguyen, the only non-Canadian on the team, focuses on operations at Mecka.
The four co-founders don’t have backgrounds in robotics. But they did recognize that there was a dearth of physical-world data and realized that capturing real-world interactions was the primary bottleneck holding back general-purpose robots, including humanoids.
Mecka, which derives its name from “mecha,” a fictional giant robot controlled by humans, set out to do for robotics what Scale AI, Mercor, Surge, and other human data companies have done for LLMs. The startup pays people to record themselves performing everyday tasks — like making coffee or fixing cars — using body sensors and smartphones.
As of early June, Mecka was projecting that it would end 2026 at an annual run rate of $100 million, Gao told Fortune when the startup announced its previous fundraise.
While Mecka AI hasn’t publicly disclosed its customer list, many robotics companies and AI labs rely on real-world data captured through this “egocentric” approach, alongside other physical data collection methods like teleoperation, to build their models.
Other startups collecting real-world data for robot training include XDOF, which TechCrunch reported last week was nearing a new round at a $1.2 billion valuation, as well as human-data platforms expanding beyond LLMs, such as Scale AI and Micro1.

Published : September 11, 2026 at 10:25 PM IST
Hyderabad: Naman Kasliwal and Shiv Patil, students of BITS Hyderabad, have developed state-of-the-art drones designed to strategically strengthen the Indian Army.
Officials announced on Thursday that the duo, who established a startup named 'Beejan', successfully tested the drones' capabilities at the KORAS laboratory within the BITS campus. Initially, they developed a software system called the 'Beejan Autonomous Navigation Module' to counter drone attacks and unauthorized drone intrusions by hostile forces. The system enables drones to reach their intended destinations without relying on GPS.
A key feature of the technology is its ability to operate effectively by penetrating through radio frequency interference. These drones have undergone experimental trials at various military centers, including Secunderabad and Leh.
Their performance was recently demonstrated to the Indian Army's Southern Command. Impressed by the technology, officials from eight other military units have also requested the system. The duo stated that the drones were built using entirely indigenous components, leveraging robotics technology and artificial intelligence.
They credited their success to the inspiration gained from finishing as runners-up in a robotics competition at IIT Bombay. Last year, their innovation won a grant of Rs 25 lakh at the 'Curiosity-2025' event held at IIT Gandhinagar.
Beijan Tech’s Prachand Swarm Ground Station software is currently deployed with formations under the Indian Army’s Southern Command, while additional applications have been developed for the Army Air Defence. The company’s autonomous navigation module has received Letters of Intent (LOIs) from eight military units.

indian-startups-7826e9230d.fulltext: Adding to the spree of UPI launches at the Global Fintech Festival (GFF) 2026 in Mumbai, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) executive director Gunveer Singh introduced a comprehensive suite of payment initiatives spanning digital ticketing, mobility payments and ecommerce. Key Innovations Unveiled at GFF 2026 Today Unified Ticketing Platform (UTP) Developed under NBBL and hosted by NTSL, the Unified Ticketing Platform integrates urban transit systems and cultural heritage sites into a standardised digital framework on Bharat Connect. The broader idea is to disparate ticketing applications, streamline merchant reconciliation and simplify route discovery for commuters and tourists. It utilises dynamic and static offline-capable QR codes to deliver instant ticketing without network lag. UTP is currently piloted with Chennai Metro Rail Limited (CMRL) for urban mass transit and the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) under the Ministry of Culture for landmark and monument entry. RuPay Credit Card on UPI International This extends India’s linked-credit UPI ecosystem to international merchant acceptance points. Travelers and overseas shoppers can scan foreign QR codes or pay international ecommerce merchants directly using their preferred UPI app linked to a RuPay credit card. The initial global corridors where this service would be rolled out would be the France, Mauritius, the UAE, and the US. It also displays real-time foreign currency amounts, live exchange rates, bank forex markup fees, and the final INR equivalent before the user enters their UPI PIN. RuPay ON-THE-GO Card-on-Device Tokenisation This is a transit payment architecture built for NFC-enabled Android smartphones to cut operational overhead for transit agencies by replacing physical plastic smartcards with instant digital onboarding. It allows commuters to issue, tokenise, and store transit credentials directly on their mobile device’s secure element and is designed for ultra-low latency environments. It allows passengers to tap-and-go at transit turnstiles even in low-connectivity underground stations. RuPay ‘Tap on Phone’ For Ecommerce The new feature brings physical contact-free card mechanics to online checkout flows. It would allow customers to tap their physical RuPay card against an NFC-enabled smartphone during mobile or web checkouts. This feature supports payments up to ₹5,000 using standard card PIN authentication, removing dependency on SMS one-time passwords (OTPs) as well as eliminating manual card entry errors, drastically cuts checkout friction, and increases transaction success rates. RuPay Passkey-Based Biometric Authentication This new authentication replaces vulnerable legacy OTPs with FIDO-aligned device-native biometric authentication. Now, cardholders could authenticate online purchases, recurring mandates, and high-value transfers using device-native fingerprints or facial recognition (face ID). It operates across iOS, Android, web browsers, as well as tokenised RuPay merchant gateways. This adds on the spree of UPI related innovations launched during the GFF 2026, with the NPCI introducing a series of digital infrastructure initiatives to expand credit access across India during the GFF 2026. The UPI operator rolled out AiNxt, an open-source, enterprise-grade agentic AI platform designed to build, test, and deploy custom intelligent agents. The suite incorporates four core components: AiNxt OS, AiNxt Code (a plugin for integrated development environments or IDEs), AiNxt CLI, and AiNxt Enterprise. These will enable development teams to build, test, and deploy across IDEs and command-line environments. The Department of Financial Services' secretary Sanjay Lohiya also unveiled open-source android ATMs to instantly issue RuPay cards and merchant UPI QR code. At the GFF 2026 inauguration, PM Narendra Modi highlighted that the next phase of UPI’s growth should focus on connecting the Indian payment system with payment ecosystems of other countries.

other-interests-1dd50842d7.headline: SpaceXAI data centre may have led to Mississippi air pollution spike
other-interests-1dd50842d7.fulltext:
Dozens of temporary gas turbines in Mississippi powering a huge SpaceXAI data centre in neighbouring Tennessee have caused a major spike in nitrogen oxide air pollution, satellite data suggests. SpaceXAI and local authorities dispute the claim.
SpaceXAI’s Colossus 2 data centre in Tennessee came online in 2025 and is now the largest operational data centre in the US, servicing the firm’s rapidly growing artificial intelligence technology.
However, the site has been embroiled in controversy over its use of temporary gas turbines. Campaigners say these turbines are contributing to hazardous levels of air pollution in the surrounding area, and there are ongoing legal cases over their use, pursued by campaigners and local residents against SpaceXAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech.
Advertisement
Normally, emissions of NOx and other air pollutants from gas power plants are controlled using catalytic converters, but most of the temporary turbines powering the Colossus 2 plant don’t have them fitted.
NOx gases can inflame the airways and exacerbate the symptoms of people already suffering from lung or heart conditions. They also react with other air pollutants to form ozone and particulate matter, both key components of urban smog.
Kevin Gauld at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and his colleagues used observations from NASA’s TEMPO satellite – launched in 2023 to monitor air pollution over North America – to assess the impact of the Colossus 2 plant on local air quality.
The satellite observations show a “strong increase” in local NOx concentrations from late 2025 onwards, according to the study by Gauld’s team, which is when SpaceXAI began deploying the temporary turbines to Colossus 2.
The researchers then used the TEMPO satellite to calculate two-week-average NOx source rates from August 2025 to mid-August 2026. They first detected NOx emissions in December 2025, and emissions increased throughout the study period. The number of turbines on the site rose during the study period, from 27 in December 2025 to 69 by August 2026.
The satellite analysis suggests that emissions averaged about 730 kilograms per hour between February and August 2026, peaking at 1180 kg per hour in August 2026. By comparison, the monthly emissions from a nearby gas power plant in Mississippi averaged just 21 kilograms per hour of NOx emissions, the paper reports.
Martyn Chipperfield at the University of Leeds in the UK, who wasn’t involved in the study, says the pollution levels observed by the satellite are significant. “The values they report in the vicinity of the [temporary turbines] are values that we have seen over central London,” he says.
Ronald Cohen at the University of California, Berkeley, says the paper is “solid” science. “It’s very clear that there’s a huge number of uncontrolled generators on this site, generators without emissions controls on them,” he says. “There’s a lot of electricity being created, and they are putting a lot of NO2 [the most commonly regulated NOx gas] into the atmosphere.”
Peter Zoogman at Minerva University, California, who worked on the development of the TEMPO satellite, says the NOx emissions, as calculated in the paper, would mean each turbine was producing roughly the same level of emissions each year as 50,000 cars. He called for further work to quantify the health impacts of the emissions, including measuring any change in the local levels of ozone pollution since the opening of the site.
In July 2026, SpaceXAI promised to remove all 69 temporary turbines by July 2027 and replace them with 41 permanent gas turbines. The company was granted permission to construct the permanent gas turbines in March 2026 by the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ). SpaceXAI also promised that all of the mobile turbines it uses – which it is starting to manufacture in-house – will be fitted with pollution-control technology.
“Making sure these converters are fitted to these power generation systems is very important,” says Zoogman. “It does make a very large difference.”
However, the satellite study concludes that the current average emissions rate from the temporary turbines is about 16 times higher than it is expected to be once the permanent turbines are installed.
Responding to queries from New Scientist, SpaceXAI sent a court submission from a third-party air-quality expert, which claims local air-quality monitoring stations haven’t observed notable increases in pollution concentrations since the mobile generators began operating. It said the emissions from the site fall within the relevant regulatory requirements.
A statement from MDEQ in response to questions from New Scientist said: “MDEQ does not comment on third-party reports or matters involved in pending litigation. MDEQ recognizes the public interest in this facility and remains committed to carrying out its responsibility to protect public health and the environment through implementation and enforcement of applicable state and federal environmental laws and regulations.”
The satellite analysis comes as concern grows over the rapid rollout of new gas power to run the massive new data centres that underpin the booming AI sector. US gas-fired power under development jumped by 50 per cent in the first half of 2026, according to Global Energy Monitor, an independent non-profit.
Meanwhile, almost half of the proposals for powering data centres with gas involve using gas turbines and engines. These are less efficient and more polluting than combined cycle plants – which reuse waste heat from one turbine to power another – but are quicker to deploy. Experts warn this new gas build-out will lock in decades of additional carbon emissions and worsen air quality. Many data centres also rely on diesel generators for back-up power, which emit high levels of NOx and other pollutants.
Data centres may also need close monitoring to check that the new dedicated power plants supporting the facilities are meeting regulatory requirements. “That’s why having this public attention on it is really valuable,” says Zoogman. “I think it’s important to have this technology to do the monitoring and the assessment and figure out where the pollution is coming from.”
Rapid advances in satellite technology mean they are increasingly being used to spot unreported emissions across a whole range of sectors, including oil and gas infrastructure, landfills and manufacturing facilities.

ai-ffccc6c522.headline: AI agents OpenAI was testing uploaded malicious software to another service, say researchers
ai-ffccc6c522.fulltext:
Agents being tested by OpenAI uploaded hundreds of malicious packages in a cyberattack on software service RubyGems in May, two months before they hacked open-source platform Hugging Face, the company confirmed Friday.
It’s the latest revelation of cyberattacks linked to major artificial intelligence developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic. The hacks or attempts to access external systems have spooked the public and heightened concerns over the increasing abilities of AI models – and whether developers can contain them.
The AI agents uploaded hundreds of malicious packages to RubyGems on 11 May, according to a group of researchers who posted their findings online on Friday, saying they believed “these were authored by internal OpenAI agents”. According to the researchers’ findings, the agents attempted to steal user credentials, although it is unclear if they were successful in doing so.
OpenAI later confirmed the incident in a statement.
“Based on our review, our agents used the RubyGems platform to access the internet to carry out benign tasks and retrieve public information. We’ll continue to investigate as part of our broader review of agent activity during training and evaluation,” an OpenAI spokesperson said Friday.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the RubyGems cyberattack.
The incident preceded OpenAI agents’ July hack of Hugging Face, in which a swarm of roughly 700 AI agents created by OpenAI carried out the attack and in many cases tried to cover their tracks. And last week, it was revealed OpenAI agents had also hijacked a German website this spring and turned it into a message board for AI agents.
Anthropic, meanwhile, has disclosed four instances of its Claude models hacking external systems.
The RubyGems revelation comes at the end of a week of intense scrutiny on AI platforms and calls to pause development until stricter safety standards can be put in place.
On Tuesday, an Anthropic researcher announced his resignation from the company on social media, warning that AI could kill off humanity within the next decade. The warnings, echoed by other Anthropic researchers, sparked calls across the political spectrum for immediate action on AI.

deep-tech-3ed9b79a1b.fulltext:
India's photonics market is projected to expand fourfold, reaching $10 billion by 2031, primarily driven by the escalating demand for high-speed data transmission within data centers and other advanced electronic devices. This significant growth positions India to potentially emerge as a global leader in photonics technology, fostering innovation and self-reliance in critical digital infrastructure.The newly established India Photonics Association (IPA), comprising 65 members including SFO Technologies, GX Quantum Photonics, Lightspeed Photonics, and Tejas Networks, is spearheading efforts to achieve this. Ashwini Aggarwal, Secretary General of the IPA, stated, "The present direct market for photonics in India is around $2.5 billion. It is expected to grow by 4 fold to $10 billion by 2031. The photonics technology will enhance speed and reliability in electronics products. We will work with industry, government and other stakeholders to make the Indian ecosystem lead the global ecosystem in photonics." He further emphasised that photonics will enhance speed and reliability in high-speed data transmission.Rohin Y, Founder and CEO of Lightspeed Photonics, highlighted India's opportune moment for innovation in this evolving technology. "India can be self-reliant in photonics technology if all efforts from industry and government are made in time. Instead of buying technology, it is time for India to catch up with the world. Industry bodies like IPA can help us collaborate and work in sync with each other," he said.Current data centers in India predominantly utilise photonics connectors supporting data transmission speeds of 10-40 gigabit per second (Gbps). However, with the advent of AI data centers, the demand for connectors capable of 100-400 Gbps will surge.In a strategic move to bolster indigenous manufacturing, broadband technology firm GX Group has announced plans to commence manufacturing operations at its advanced photonics facility from December this year. The company has earmarked an investment of ₹500 crore for this facility in India. GX Group has secured government approval for phase 1 of the plant, which will focus on producing Optical Transceiver SFPs (small form-factor pluggable). These components are crucial for converting electrical signals into optical signals and vice-versa, enabling high-speed networks.Sambit Swain, Director Global Sales at GX Group, underscored the technology's foundational role. "Photonics is becoming the backbone of digital and semiconductor future. The Indian Photonics Association is a welcome step that will unite industry, academia and policymakers to drive innovation, indigenous manufacturing, talent and global partnerships. The association will pave the way for a strong, globally competitive Indian photonics ecosystem and position India as a global photonics hub," Swain said.

New Delhi, Sep 11 (KNN) Google on Thursday announced five new sustainability and clean-energy initiatives in India covering rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, climate-smart farming, climate technology research and AI-led climate innovation.
The initiatives will use artificial intelligence (AI), geospatial data and satellite technology to support India's clean energy transition and climate goals.

The Google Center for Climate Technology has selected three initial projects focused on green workforce training and low-carbon construction materials. It has also added water stewardship and waste and circularity as new focus areas.

Disha Aggarwal, a senior programme lead at the energy think tank CEEW, was quoted by Reuters saying India needs to fast-track battery storage commissioning so surplus solar generation can be used at night. Reuters also reported outages and complaints in New Delhi, Noida, and the state of Odisha during the same heatwave period.
Capacity mix versus generation mix
In an Aug. 17, 2026 commentary, Reuters columnist Gavin Maguire wrote that data from Ember and Global Energy Monitor showed India's clean energy installed capacity had reached 331.7 gigawatts, compared with 302.0 gigawatts of fossil fuel capacity, giving clean power a majority share of installed capacity for the first time. The same commentary noted that coal still accounts for roughly 70% of actual electricity generation because coal plants run continuously while solar output is intermittent. Solar capacity alone stood at 211 gigawatts as of the report, up from 0.07 gigawatts in 2010, per Ember data cited in the column. Between 2025 and mid-2026, India added 75.5 gigawatts of solar capacity compared with 3.8 gigawatts of coal capacity, according to the same Reuters commentary.
Separately, a Bloomberg India Edition newsletter published Aug. 13, 2026 described rising electricity demand in India as tied to climate-driven temperature extremes and growing power use from digital infrastructure, including data centers.
Distribution as a longstanding constraint
A 2014 World Bank diagnostic review of India's power sector said persistent operational and financial shortcomings in electricity distribution represented a core weakness for the sector, noting that revenue for the entire power value chain originates with customers at the distribution level. The report is more than a decade old, but its focus on distribution as the constraint through which new generation and storage capacity must be delivered and billed remains relevant to current discussions of grid reliability.
MarketScale analysis
MarketScale analysis: For companies operating in India with evening-heavy electricity use, the reported gap between installed solar capacity and evening supply reliability may be worth monitoring alongside contract terms for backup power and demand response, though no timeline for closing that gap has been reported.

climate-energy-afcf5def73.headline: Department of Commerce finalizes trade duties on solar imports from India, Indonesia, and Laos
climate-energy-afcf5def73.fulltext:
Department of Commerce finalizes trade duties on solar imports from India, Indonesia, and Laos
The U.S. Department of Commerce has issued final affirmative determinations in its antidumping and countervailing duty investigations targeting crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells and modules imported from India, Indonesia, and Laos.
Commerce reported a finding that manufacturers in all three nations dumped solar components into the U.S. market below fair value and benefited from government subsidies, resulting in material injury to the domestic solar manufacturing sector. The decision marks the conclusion of the Department of Commerce phase of the Solar IV trade litigation, originally brought by the Alliance for American Solar Manufacturing and Trade. Find an International Trade Administration fact sheet here.
In its final determination, Commerce established steep dumping margins and countervailing subsidy rates across mandatory respondents and all other producers in the targeted nations.
For Indian suppliers, Commerce calculated final dumping margins at 123.04% for all producers, alongside a countervailing duty rate set at 126.09%. Indonesian exporters face finalized dumping margins at 94.36% for all producers, with final countervailing duty rates ranging between 73.2% and 173.7%, depending on the specific manufacturer. For imports originating in Laos, Commerce set final dumping margins at 65.43% for all exporters, accompanied by countervailing subsidy rates established between 82.03% and 153.67%.
Unlike broader statutory actions like reciprocal tariffs or Section 232 national security measures, the trade measures are case-specific orders under the Tariff Act of 1930. The final antidumping and countervailing duties will stack directly on top of existing executive tariffs rather than replacing them.
The cases were initiated following petitions from the Alliance for American Solar Manufacturing and Trade, a coalition represented by lead petitioners First Solar, Hanwha Qcells USA, and Mission Solar Energy.
“America’s solar manufacturing sector is poised for a historic resurgence, with domestic module capacity up more than 750% since 2022 and cell production expanding as well,” said Tim Brightbill, co-chair of Wiley’s International Trade Practice and lead counsel to the Alliance. “But that progress is being harmed by dumped and subsidized imports from India, Indonesia, and Laos that have denied American producers a level playing field. Today’s final determinations are an essential step toward enforcing our trade laws and restoring fair competition for U.S. solar manufacturers and the workers they employ.”
Market context
While the Solar IV cases conclude, the market reality on the ground has already shifted. Cell procurement for U.S. module assembly has largely migrated away from the target nations, with primary cell volumes now originating in South Korea, the Philippines, and emerging African manufacturing hubs including Kenya, Nigeria, and Ethiopia. Meanwhile, South Korean cell suppliers face their own trade headwinds following a separate trade petition filed by the coalition American Manufacturers for Energy Resilience.
These finalized duties also arrive alongside structural administrative changes reshaping solar procurement. Federal trade rules recently established Section 232 minimum import price floors across the supply chain, setting statutory minimum entry prices of $21 per kilogram for raw polysilicon, $100 per kilogram for ingots and wafers, $0.22 per watt for solar cells, and $0.38 per watt for modules.
With government-mandated price floors governing imported components, industry observers note that the legal foundation for future antidumping and countervailing duty cases may lessen significantly. Because minimum import prices administratively dictate the baseline cost of foreign solar goods, proving that domestic manufacturers suffer material injury from unfair undercutting or dumped pricing becomes substantially harder to substantiate under U.S. trade law standards.
Next steps
The determination follows the U.S. International Trade Commission final hearing held earlier this week. The proceedings now turn to the Commission for its final injury vote, scheduled for October 14, 2026, to determine whether dumped and subsidized imports from the three nations materially injure or threaten the U.S. solar manufacturing industry.
If the International Trade Commission vote is affirmative, Commerce will issue official duty orders on November 2, 2026, imposing the finalized cash deposit rates. If the panel finds no material injury, the proceedings will terminate and all cash deposits previously collected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection will be refunded.
The Solar IV cases follow the implementation of Solar III duty orders in June 2025 targeting imports from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam, which saw shipments from those four nations fall from $12.2 billion in 2023 to $1.3 billion in 2025.

BMW India Sees Little Scope for Hybrids, Expects Diesel to Lose Out as EVs Gain
The German carmaker rules out plug-in hybrids citing cabin packaging compromises and long-range battery gains, as EVs reach 26% of local sales.
BMW India sees little scope for hybrid vehicles in its portfolio as electric vehilcles gain faster acceptance in the luxury segment, although the broader passenger vehicle market is pursuing a mix of powertrain technologies.
According to BMW India President and CEO Hardeep Singh Brar, the improvement in driving range of electric vehicles had weakened the case for combining an electric motor with a petrol engine.
“Because when EVs give you a range of 728 km, you put petrol engine and hybrid system also, the power, the acceleration figures for a plug-in hybrid are very, very pathetic. You won't like driving a plug-in hybrid,” Brar said.
He said hybrids also add weight and take away cabin space because they combine a battery and an engine.
“And you also increase the weight of the car [hybrid powertrain]. It also takes away your space. Having [both] a battery and engine, you are somewhere compromising on the space,” he said.
“So, it doesn't make sense,” Brar said, when asked why BMW does not have hybrids in its portfolio.
BMW India’s aggressive push in electric mobility has emerged as the biggest driver behind its rise to the top of India’s luxury car market, with electric vehicles accounting for more than a quarter of its sales in the first half of 2026.
The automaker sold 2,359 electric vehicles between January and June, registering a 78% year-on-year growth. EVs contributed 26% of BMW Group India’s total sales, up from 21% a year ago, reinforcing its position as the country's largest luxury EV brand with a 69% market share in the segment.
The luxury vehicle segment is seeing faster adoption of electric cars. This contrasts with the mass passenger vehicle market, where automakers are pursuing a multi-fuel strategy involving EVs, hybrids, CNG and biofuels. EV penetration in the mass-market passenger vehicle segment is around 7%.
Brar said BMW continues to offer diesel vehicles across its portfolio despite a decline in demand, with the company assessing powertrain demand by segment.
“For example, in this category [7 Series'], we didn't see diesel demand at all,” he said.
BMW India reported a 5 percentage-point increase in the share of electric vehicles in its sales in the first half, while diesel declined by 3 percentage points and petrol by 2 percentage points, Brar said.
On government policy, Brar said central and state governments need to follow a more aligned approach on vehicle taxation. He said state-level taxes create disruption while the central government has a common GST structure for cars.
“State governments have to align with what the central government is doing,” Brar said. “State governments are not really aligned with the central government. They are moving in their own direction.”
He cited Delhi as an example, saying the capital has a 10% tax compared with 5% in Haryana and zero in Uttar Pradesh, prompting customers to register vehicles outside Delhi.
“Delhi is one of the most polluted states in the world. And secondly, you didn't make high revenue because customers are moving out,” he said.If you want, I can also make this tighter and more Reuters-like at exactly 450 words, while retaining all the requested points and exact quotes.
BMW is also increasing local manufacturing and sourcing. Brar said 95% of BMW's 13 models in India are localised, with completely built units accounting for 5%. He said the company is looking to further increase localisation as it expands its portfolio.

health-tech-98ce62fd2b.headline: Weekly Rundown: Cleveland Clinic taps Luminai for AI automation; Quest brings lab testing to Apple Health
health-tech-98ce62fd2b.fulltext:
Stay up to date on the latest in health tech, digital health and health AI news with this weekly brief. Read below for news from the week of Sept. 7 to 11.
Suki launches research initiative for healthcare AI
Ambient clinical intelligence platform Suki announced Thursday the launch of an industry-wide scientific research initiative geared towards generating research and clinical evidence to advance healthcare AI.
The new initiative—dubbed Science at Sukii—coincides with the new Suki Research Collaborative (SRC), a research network comprised of health systems and academic institutions. The collaborative plans to study AI’s implementation, workflow optimization, specialty care and more.
      
      
SRC Chair Sudha Jayaraman, M.D., said in a statement that the future of ambient clinical intelligence “won't be defined solely” by technological breakthroughs, but by “the quality of the evidence behind them.”
"By bringing together leading clinicians, researchers, engineers, and health systems to generate objective evidence, we're helping healthcare organizations adopt Ambient Clinical Intelligence with the confidence needed to improve patient care, support clinicians, and advance the practice of medicine,” Jayaraman said.
Apple Health teams up with Quest Diagnostics for lab tests
Apple announced an expansion of its health and fitness capabilities Wednesday, including new offerings from its Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.
      
New Apple Watch products have a Health Sensing System, which the company says enables the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable. The watches also have a readiness capability, which analyzes users’ biometrics—like recent activity and sleep score—to provide a score ranked zero through 10 for each day.
“At Apple, we believe technology can empower everyone with actionable, science-based insights built with privacy at the core. By combining breakthrough sensing on Apple Watch with Apple Intelligence in the Health app, we’re able to translate complex biometric data into clear guidance for users,” said Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, in a statement. “This both helps people navigate their day-to-day routines with confidence and connects those moments with deeper context around their longevity, building a strong foundation for a healthier future.”
Another new capability the tech giant announced is lab services. Through the Health app, users can schedule and purchase new labs featuring more than 50 key biomarkers for $119 at approximately 2,000 Quest Diagnostics locations across the nation.
Cleveland Clinic taps Luminai for AI automation
Cleveland Clinic and Luminai are partnering to co-develop and deploy AI automation across administrative workflows, the organizations announced Wednesday.
Luminai’s engineering team will work alongside Cleveland Clinic’s clinical and operational staff to deploy the workflows rather than a standardized configuration.
The first priority area for the partnership is external referral processing. Luminai's platform identifies referrals, understands clinical context, matches the type and transcribes documents into electronic medical records (EMRs) for follow-up, the company says.
“Automation only delivers value when it reflects the realities of clinical and operational work,” said Rohit Chandra, Ph.D., Cleveland Clinic chief digital officer, in a statement. “Our collaboration with Luminai allows us to apply AI in ways that meaningfully support our teams by reducing administrative burden and improving patient satisfaction.”
FDA names inaugural AI deputy commissioner
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced Tuesday a slew of new leadership appointments at the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), including the first Deputy Commissioner for Technology and Artificial Intelligence.
Jared Seehafer was selected for the role and will serve as the agency’s leader on technology, software and AI. He will also establish agency-wide strategies and priorities in these areas.
Seehafer has two decades of technical and leadership experience.
      
The appointment “underscores” the current administration’s commitment to “accelerating reliable AI innovation, modernizing federal technology, and ensuring an effective regulatory framework for emerging technologies,” according to a Sept. 8 press release.
Jacksonville, Fla.-based Mayo Clinic to implement Rainfall Health platform
AI-powered compliance and reimbursement platform Rainfall Health announced Wednesday it will be implemented across a Mayo Clinic facility to support care coordination and compliance associated with the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM).
CMS selected 721 hospitals to participate in the first cohort of TEAM, which is a mandatory payment model dedicated to improving quality and coordination of care. TEAM launched Jan. 1.
Rainfall’s AI platform allows organizations to coordinate care, monitor patient progress and automate workflows associated with value-based care (VBC) models. The platform will be used to support post-acute care coordination and quality reporting efforts for participating patients, the organizations say.
“This news reflects the growing demand for AI-enabled solutions that help hospitals succeed under value-based care models,” said Eddie Qureshi, Rainfall Health CEO and founder, in a statement. “Healthcare organizations participating in CMS's evolving value-based care models are looking for scalable ways to coordinate care, improve operational efficiency, and meet reporting requirements. Rainfall stands ready to help systems navigate these changes while supporting quality patient care.”

The amount invested (on R&D on seeds) should remain steady or increase,” Kaan told a select group of reporters.
    
Post October 1, 2026, Corteva would be split into two distinct publicly-listed entities globally. One will handle the crop protection business which will continue to carry the brand name Corteva. The other Vylor (earlier called SpinCo), will carry on its seeds and genetics business.

On India plans, Kaan said that as its licensing business expands in the country, there is potential for small Indian companies to access this technology. It could also be incorporated into their own business plans and help farmers and customers
    
“We are working with Indian companies to access good wheat germplasm and then bring in our technology from overseas. The objective is to eventually develop advanced wheat hybrids that are significantly higher-yielding than existing varieties. We will continue to invest significantly in India,” Kaan added.
    
He said the company, which has a very strong asset in India in the form of Hyderabad-based Multi Crop Research Centre, would continue to invest significantly in the country. It is Corteva’s second-most technologically advanced R&D facility outside the US.
    
“We review our licensing strategy all the time. I do not expect it to change substantially, except that in the future we could bring gene editing into the licensing business. This is in addition to licensing actual seeds to local companies,” Kaan said.
    
He said the company would also like to bring more gene-edited licensed products into India.
    
“As an example, there are tomatoes in Japan. More recently, International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT) announced that it has a licence from us (Corteva) for gene editing and is looking at climate-resilient rice across Asia and Africa. There is also work on pigeon pea. The technology (gene editing) is not limited to particular crops. It is about the trait or attribute you are looking for in a plant,” Kaan added.
    
He said for India, it is an exciting technology because it can help with adaptation to new climates, heat, water challenges and shorter growing periods, allowing farmers to produce more from each acre.
    
“We expect to see rapid growth in adoption of the technology as regulatory pathways become clearer around the world,” Kaan said.
    
On the regulatory regime in India and the new Seeds Bill, Kaan said that as the company invests heavily in R&D, it wants to make sure there is a stable and consistent return on that investment without too many surprises.
    
He said directionally the Seeds Bill is ‘positive’, though there may be some details we could change.
    
“The most important thing for us is that the central government is moving towards a system where farmers are allowed to farm and make their own choices. Our biggest priority in any legislation is that farmers need the ability to choose what is best for them. They should be able to choose what they grow, when they grow it and how they grow it. That is very central to us,” Kaan added.

agritech-b76533ed88.headline: From Food Security to AI: ASEAN-India Sets a New Course for Agricultural Cooperation
agritech-b76533ed88.fulltext:
From Food Security to AI: ASEAN-India Sets a New Course for Agricultural Cooperation
11 September 2026, New Delhi: ASEAN and India have agreed to strengthen cooperation on digital agriculture, climate-resilient farming and agricultural value chains as they seek to make regional food systems more resilient to climate, trade and supply-chain disruptions.
The priorities emerged from the Ninth ASEAN-India Ministerial Meeting on Agriculture and Forestry (9th AIMMAF), held in New Delhi on 9 September 2026.
The meeting identified artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, machine learning, soil health, bio-inputs, climate-resilient crops and low-emission rice production among the areas where ASEAN and India could expand practical cooperation.
The countries are also looking to strengthen the movement of agricultural products and inputs across the region, with greater emphasis on post-harvest management, value-added processing, food-loss reduction and agricultural logistics.
New Plan to Drive Cooperation
The discussions set the stage for the ASEAN-India Medium-Term Plan of Action for Cooperation in Agriculture and Forestry 2026-2030, which will guide the next phase of collaboration.
The plan is structured around four broad priorities: food security and resilient value chains; digital innovation and information exchange; technology cooperation and joint research; and capacity building, farmer exchanges and inclusive rural enterprises.
The shift comes as agriculture across the region faces a combination of climate risks, extreme weather, geopolitical tensions, volatile fertiliser and energy prices, trade disruptions and threats from plant pests and animal diseases.
ASEAN and India said stronger regional cooperation will be needed to maintain the flow of food and critical agricultural inputs, including fertilisers, seeds and pesticides.
The countries also called for greater diversification of supply sources and stronger regional monitoring and early-warning systems.
AI Moves Higher on Agriculture Agenda
Digital technologies are emerging as a key component of the next phase of ASEAN-India agricultural cooperation.
The proposed areas include the use of AI, IoT and machine learning for precision agriculture, alongside digital agriculture and forestry applications.
The meeting also stressed that technology development must be better connected with farmers and agricultural extension systems. Research institutions, technology providers, private companies and farmers’ organisations will need to work more closely to move innovations from laboratories and pilot projects into wider farm-level adoption.
The focus on practical deployment is intended to address one of the persistent challenges in agricultural technology: turning new digital and scientific tools into solutions that farmers can use at scale.
Climate-Resilient Production in Focus
Climate adaptation and lower-emission production will also feature prominently in the new cooperation agenda.
Potential areas include low-emission rice production, improved water productivity, climate-resilient and nutritious crops, sustainable soil management and bio-inputs.
ASEAN and India are also looking to expand cooperation on alternatives to open crop-residue burning and circular bioeconomy solutions, linking agricultural productivity with environmental goals.
The countries’ earlier cooperation included the ASEAN-India Millets Festivals in Jakarta and New Delhi in 2023, which promoted millets for their nutritional and climate-resilience benefits.
Stronger Food and Agricultural Value Chains
Beyond production, ASEAN and India are putting greater emphasis on what happens after crops leave the farm.
The meeting called for stronger cooperation in post-harvest management, preservation technologies, value-added processing and food-loss and waste reduction.
Improved logistics and market connectivity are also expected to support more efficient movement and distribution of agricultural and forestry products.
The agenda extends to forestry, including sustainable forest management, landscape restoration, agroforestry, forest monitoring and responsible forest-based value chains.
From Policy Dialogue to Implementation
The meeting said the next step will be to translate the 2026-2030 plan into a results-oriented work programme with clear priorities, responsible agencies, expected outputs and timelines.
Research and education institutions, farmer organisations, cooperatives, MSMEs, private companies, financial institutions and development partners are expected to play a role in implementation.
ASEAN and India have already built cooperation through the previous 2021-2025 action plan, which covered food security, sustainable and climate-resilient agriculture, soil management, digitalisation, science and technology and institutional exchanges.
The ASEAN-India Fellowship for Higher Education in Agriculture and Allied Sciences, launched in 2024, provides 50 Master’s fellowships over five years for students from ASEAN Member States.
The ninth ministerial meeting concluded with an agreement to convene the 10th ASEAN-India Ministerial Meeting on Agriculture and Forestry in 2028, giving the two sides a new milestone to assess progress on their expanded agriculture agenda.

indian-startups-936b76647e.headline: Mitti Labs Enters Deal With Google For 1 Mn Carbon Credits
indian-startups-936b76647e.fulltext: Climate tech startup Mitti Labs has signed a four-year agreement with Google to supply 1 Mn Carbon credits till 2030, which it describes as one of the largest nature-based offtakes to date The financial terms of the agreement have not been disclosed. However, Mitti Labs said the deal is a fixed contractual offtake covering 1 Mn credits, delivered between 2027 and 2030. Mitti Labs said payments will be made upon delivery of the verified carbon credits, with no upfront financing involved in the agreement. The credits will primarily be generated from Mitti Labs’ rice farming projects in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka. The startup currently has programmes covering more than 1 Lakh hectares in India. “We are currently working on expanding both across India and Southeast Asia. This deal with Google doesn't just validate the quality of the projects, the use of our MRV and the scalability of our projects, but will also help us scale our India projects,” cofounder Xavier Laguarta Soler told Inc42. Kate Brandt, Google’s chief sustainability officer, said Mitti Labs’ approach could cut methane emissions while conserving water and helping smallholder farmers adopt more efficient irrigation practices. “Mitti Labs' approach delivers critical near-term atmospheric impact by cutting methane emissions, while conserving billions of gallons of water and empowering smallholder farmers to deploy advanced water-management practices. We’re excited to partner with them to help accelerate and scale their solution across India,” Brandt said. The agreement comes a month after Mitti Labs raised $9.5 Mn in a Series A round led by Aramco Ventures. The funding is being used to expand its operations across India and develop new greenfield projects in the Philippines and Indonesia. Cutting Methane By Changing How Rice Is Grown Rice farming is a major Methane producer, a potent greenhouse gas. Flooding fields creates oxygen-poor conditions in which methane-producing microbes thrive. Mitti Labs works with farmers to introduce a practice known as alternate wetting and drying (AWD). Developed by the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI), the technique involves allowing fields to dry periodically before they are irrigated again. The approach can reduce the conditions that produce methane while using less water, as per Mitti Labs, without affecting crop yields. Mitti Labs trains farmers and provides support as they adopt the practice. It also shares revenue from the resulting carbon credits with participating farming communities. Mitti Labs’ AI platform combines high-resolution synthetic aperture radar, remote sensing and biogeochemical models with on-the-ground measurements to estimate changes in greenhouse gas emissions and water use. Water savings are also measured using flow meters. The GeoAI platform has been developed with support from NASA through a grant. Mitti Labs has also begun expanding outside India, with the Philippines serving as its first south-east Asian pilot market. It is exploring other major rice-producing markets in the region.

indian-startups-551a344be7.headline: AI-native patient safety startup Graph AI raises $13.3 million in funding from Insight Partners
indian-startups-551a344be7.fulltext:
Graph AI, a startup developing AI software for pharmaceutical patient safety operations, has raised $13.3 million in a Series A funding round led by Insight Partners.
Existing investor Bessemer Venture Partners also took part in the financing, which Graph AI said will support its expansion across the US and Europe.
The latest investment follows a $3 million seed round led by Bessemer in October 2025.
Founded in 2024, Graph AI develops Graph Safety, a platform intended to automate parts of pharmacovigilance, the monitoring and management of potential safety problems associated with medicines.
The startup said pharmaceutical safety teams still spend significant amounts of time on manual processing and operational tasks.
Graph Safety combines AI with predetermined controls, validation layers and end-to-end audit trails, with the aim of allowing source data and system outputs to be traced and reviewed by people.
The startup claims that in live deployments its software had reduced the time taken to process safety cases from more than three hours to less than 10 minutes, while cutting operating costs by as much as 66%.
Raghav Parvataraju, CEO of Graph AI, said pharmacovigilance had traditionally dealt with growing case volumes by adding staff and processes around older systems.
“We believe intelligence can change that. Graph Safety gives safety experts an intelligent system that takes on operational complexity, while keeping traceability, accountability, and human oversight at the center. We are not replacing human judgment, we are building technology that allows experts to apply it where it matters most,” he said.
Graph AI has brought two modules to market since its seed round.
Its Intake module is designed to capture and triage incoming reports of adverse events across different channels, while Nucleus is a safety database that automates case processing.
A third module, Report, which is designed to automate aggregate safety reporting, is due to launch in September.
The startup is also working on Signal, a planned module intended to identify emerging safety signals and patterns across cases.
It had onboarded pharmaceutical and biotechnology customers in North America and other markets, and had secured design partnerships for modules still under development.
Richard Matus, principal at Insight Partners, said pharmaceutical companies needed to manage patient safety accurately but generally did not want to integrate a range of separate systems themselves.
“We believe that's a perfect problem for an AI team that lives inside this industry with complete focus,” he said.
“Patient safety should run an intelligent, integrated platform, not fragmented tools and manual handoffs,” he said.
Graph AI said Graph Safety had been designed with reference to applicable regulatory requirements and changing expectations around the use of AI in medicines development and patient safety.
The startup cited the US Food and Drug Administration's framework for assessing the credibility of AI models used to support regulatory decision-making. That framework forms part of draft FDA guidance and contains non-binding recommendations.
It also cited the European Union's AI Act and a report published by the Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences' Working Group XIV on the use of AI in pharmacovigilance.

india-deep-tech-e4bcb71901.headline: From AI to Directed Energy, DRDO Advances Indigenous Border Surveillance and Counter-Drone Techs for India's Smarter Border Security
india-deep-tech-e4bcb71901.fulltext:
India is accelerating the development of a highly advanced, automated security network to protect its vast and complex borders.
Spearheading this initiative is the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), which is creating a suite of homegrown technologies—ranging from artificial intelligence (AI) to directed-energy weapons—aimed at detecting, tracking, and neutralising threats.
In a recent interview, Dr. B.K. Das, Director General of Electronics and Communication Systems at DRDO, explained that relying on physical infrastructure like fences is no longer enough.
The future of border security lies in robust, electronic systems. To achieve this, DRDO is building an end-to-end security chain packed with next-generation innovations.
A Multi-Layered Surveillance Network
To catch intruders before they can cause harm, DRDO is developing high-tech detection systems. These include fibre-optic sensors, high-resolution and infrared cameras, as well as hyperspectral and multispectral imaging tools.
For round-the-clock monitoring regardless of weather conditions, advanced radar networks and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) systems are being integrated.
Dr. Das emphasised that these sensors will be backed by a highly secure and powerful communication infrastructure. This ensures that the moment a threat is detected, the information is instantly relayed across the security network for rapid action.
Tackling the Drone Threat
One of the most critical challenges on the modern battlefield is the rise of rogue drones used for smuggling, reconnaissance, and attacks.
To counter this, DRDO has already developed its first generation of counter-drone technologies, such as the D4 Anti-Drone System, which has been transferred to Indian industries like Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) for mass production and deployed in sensitive areas.
These systems use a combination of radar, electro-optical sensors, and radio frequency detectors to spot and identify suspicious drones. Once identified, the system can choose between two methods to eliminate the threat:
- Soft Kill: Disrupting the drone's electronics or jamming its communication and GPS signals.
- Hard Kill: Physically destroying the drone using directed-energy weapons (DEWs), such as high-powered lasers.
The Role of Artificial Intelligence
To manage this complex web of sensors and weapons, DRDO is heavily investing in AI and machine learning.
These smart algorithms will help quickly determine whether an incoming object is a friend or foe (IFF) and aid military commanders in making split-second decisions.
As advanced radar analysis improves, AI will play a central role in filtering out the noise and identifying genuine threats.
Achieving Complete Self-Reliance
A major objective for DRDO is cutting India's dependence on foreign military imports.
Dr. Das pointed out that maintaining control over core technologies—such as radar chips, detection algorithms, and optical sensors—will give India a "decisive edge" in any future conflict.
"Sooner, all the systems will be completely indigenous, with more power and more autonomy," Das stated, highlighting that true border security comes when soldiers can fully trust weapons and technologies designed and built within their own country.
Over the next decade, India's border defences are set to transform from traditional wire fencing into an invisible, AI-driven shield dominated by electronic warfare and smart surveillance.

india-fb27f23db4.fulltext:
India launched its first 
Aadhaar card
 in 2010. And sixteen years later, the Aadhaar card which has now become an integral part of important documentation work in the country is now set to go global.
The 
Unique Identification Authority of India
 (
UIDAI
) is working towards expanding Aadhaar beyond India, with a particular focus on allowing non-resident Indians and overseas citizens of India to benefit from the country's digital identification system, a senior official said on Thursday.
Speaking during a fireside chat at Global Fintech Fest 2026, UIDAI CEO Saurabh Vijay said his objective is to build Aadhaar into a best-in-class digital identity infrastructure that can support its expansion internationally.
Aadhaar Card To Go Global
"I think for Aadhaar, the focus now is making Aadhaar international. We really want to work on the interoperability part of it -- how to make it more possible. So already some PoCs (proof of concept) are happening.
"Our legal framework is also going (in that direction) to make Aadhaar international. We are working on policies to make it (available) for overseas citizens of India (OCIs) so that it brings in more investment," PTI reported him saying.
Vijay also pointed out that the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) had launched three products at the event, adding that some of these could eventually be taken to international markets.
UIDAI works closely with NPCI to provide authentication for financial transactions.
The authority is also preparing guidelines that would allow small merchants to use Aadhaar-enabled authentication for KYC (know your customer) processes, Vijay said.
According to him, Aadhaar-based digital KYC has made customer onboarding easier and has also helped reduce the time taken for onboarding by UIDAI partners.
"We are working towards reducing this whole journey and making it more seamless with new products, something like Aadhaar Lite. The guidelines will be out very soon. Already it has been a work in progress," Vijay said.
Aadhaar Card
Aadhaar is a 12-digit randomly generated identification number issued by the UIDAI to residents of India after completion of the verification process prescribed by it.
Any person who is a resident of India can voluntarily enrol for Aadhaar, regardless of age or gender. The enrolment process is completely free and requires the individual to provide limited demographic and biometric information.
A person only needs to enrol for Aadhaar once. Following demographic and biometric de-duplication, only one Aadhaar number is generated for an individual. The de-duplication process ensures that each Aadhaar number is unique.
Demographic information
The demographic details collected during enrolment include:
- Name
- Date of Birth (verified) or Age (declared)
- Gender
- Address
- Mobile Number (optional)
- Email ID (optional)
For enrolment based on the Head of Family, the information also includes the name of the Head of Family, the relationship and the Head of Family’s Aadhaar number.
In the case of a child’s enrolment, the details required include the Enrolment ID or Aadhaar number of either parent and a Proof of Relationship (PoR) document.
Biometric information
The biometric information collected consists of:
- Ten fingerprints
- Two iris scans
- Facial photograph
According to UIDAI, Aadhaar can be verified online in a cost-effective manner. Its unique identification and de-duplication capabilities are designed to prevent duplicate and fake identities.
The number can also serve as a basis or primary identifier for implementing various government welfare schemes and programmes, helping improve service delivery, transparency and governance.
The programme is described as unique globally because it provides a state-of-the-art digital and online identity free of cost to people on such a large scale. It also has the potential to transform how services are delivered across the country.
An Aadhaar number does not contain any intelligence and is not designed to profile individuals on the basis of caste, religion, income, health or geography. While Aadhaar serves as proof of identity, possessing an Aadhaar number does not establish citizenship or domicile.
Aadhaar is also positioned as a policy instrument for social and financial inclusion, reforms in public sector service delivery, fiscal budget management and greater convenience for people. It is intended to support hassle-free, people-centric governance.
The Aadhaar number can function as a permanent Financial Address and support financial inclusion among underprivileged and weaker sections of society. In this context, it is also regarded as an instrument of distributive justice and equality.
The Aadhaar identity platform is one of the key pillars of ‘Digital India’, providing every resident of the country with a unique identity. The programme has crossed several milestones and is the world's largest biometrics-based identification system.
With features such as uniqueness, authentication, Financial Address and e-KYC, the Aadhaar identity platform enables the government to directly reach residents while delivering a range of subsidies, benefits and services using the resident's Aadhaar number.

world-d17da58776.fulltext:
The student behind 'cockroach' protests that forced an Indian minister to quit
- Published
In just under three months, 30-year-old Abhijeet Dipke - the founder and face of India's Gen Z "cockroach" protests - has acquired the kind of celebrity status normally reserved for a breakout actor or cricketer.
In politics or activism, unless you come from an influential family, such recognition can take years - if it comes at all.
"It's been a rollercoaster ride. Two-three months ago, nobody knew me. I was just in my room in Boston watching documentaries or attending lectures," said Dipke, who recently completed a master's in public relations at Boston University.
"Now I'm here surrounded by hundreds of people, by cameras. It's a bit overwhelming."
In and around his hometown of Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar in the western state of Maharashtra, Dipke is routinely thronged by people wanting to shake his hand or take a photo.
If the attention bothers him, it doesn't show. Perhaps because politics isn't entirely new to him: before moving to the US, Dipke had worked with the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), an opposition party that grew out of an anti-corruption movement, for three years.
Then, on 16 May, Dipke wrote a post on X that would change his life: "What if all cockroaches come together?"
It was a response to a remark by India's Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to cockroaches. Kant later said his comments had been misinterpreted and were directed specifically at young people using fake degrees, rather than the country's youth more broadly.
But the clarification did little to quell the outrage.
Dipke said he wrote his post while playing a video game. "It was totally spontaneous. I had no idea it would become such a big movement," he said.
Encouraged by tens of thousands of responses, he joined a handful of former colleagues and activists to launch the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), its name playing on both the chief justice's remark and that of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Alongside the support, Dipke and the campaign were fiercely trolled by government supporters. Their website and X account was briefly taken down in India.
Dipke says that when he wrote to X and to India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology asking why the account had been taken down, he received a notice saying it had been withheld under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act which allows the government to block online information 'in the interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State'.
The ministry did not reply to the BBC's questions about the issue, but The Indian Express and other media reported government officials as saying the sites had been blocked because of 'national security concerns'. Dipke says he decided to return to India in response to this.
"I took the decision to come back to India when I was called a national security threat by my own government. That really hurt me. Isn't my government supposed to stand by me when I'm abroad?" he said.
"I decided I need to go back to my country to show I'm not a national security threat. I love my country, just not in the way that you [the government] want."
Returning was not an easy decision. In recent years, activists and journalists critical of the government have faced police questioning, legal cases and, in some instances, jail.
Dipke says a lawyer he consulted advised him against returning, warning that he could be detained under the National Security Act (NSA), which allows detention without formal charge or trial. The government has always denied it takes retaliatory action but a fear of reprisal prevails.
"I won't lie. I was afraid. I had sleepless nights thinking if I go back to India, my life will change. But if I sit in the US, all these people who have followed the Cockroach Janta Party, they will feel betrayed - that 'he didn't come to India, he just kept hiding in the US'," said Dipke.
His family was worried too.
"My mother broke down over a phone call. She said, 'Why are you coming back? They might put you in jail or attack you.' I told her I can't backtrack now because people will mock me."
The cockroach protests were not the first mass agitation Modi's government has faced. Thousands protested against a controversial citizenship law in 2019 and against farm laws introduced in 2020.
Those movements were often portrayed by government supporters as representing particular religious or political interests, or as attempts to damage India's image.
Attempts to discredit the cockroach protests in similar ways, however, gained less traction for a number of reasons.
Despite India's impressive economic growth, education and employment remain major concerns for young Indians. A recent government report found that just over 8% of graduates find jobs aligned with their skills. The unemployment rate for graduates stands at 29.1% - a rate nine times higher than for those who never attended school.
And after more than 12 years in power, Modi's government is facing anti-incumbency in a way it didn't back in 2020.
But, crucially, the CJP also found an issue with broad appeal.
Around the time the campaign began, the national medical entrance exam was scrapped after a question-paper leak. The scandal resonated with students and middle-class families, cutting across religious and caste lines. More than 20 students were reported to have taken their own lives in its aftermath.
Dipke says focusing on the leak was not a strategic decision, but a response to students who reached out to the CJP.
"I was speaking to at least a hundred followers every day, and most of them were complaining about the paper leak. There was this core frustration around it," he said.
When the CJP first protested at Delhi's Jantar Mantar on 6 June, the turnout was in hundreds, but nowhere near enough for it to be considered a serious movement on the ground.
"But the longer we sat, the more people started trusting us," Dipke said. He credits activist Sonam Wangchuk's 26-day hunger strike for galvanising support.
Then came a turning point.
On 20 July, when protesters attempted to march towards parliament, police and paramilitary forces used tear gas, batons and pellet guns to disperse them. Dozens of protesters were injured; the government says dozens of police personnel were also wounded.
Images of young protesters being met with force triggered a surge of support. Thousands began arriving at Jantar Mantar and demonstrations spread to other cities.
Opposition parties rallied behind the CJP. Asked whether he challenged their leaders over why they had not taken up students' concerns more forcefully, Dipke said he had not.
"This was the first time I was organising a protest so I was just grateful to them for coming out in support of us."
The government was suddenly on the back foot. On two successive nights, Modi released videos addressing the country's youth, saying that tough action would be taken against those involved in exam leaks. But they fuelled further backlash because he wasn't offering what the protesters wanted: the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
It seemed almost unthinkable that Pradhan, a core BJP leader who had played an important role in recent regional elections, would be compelled to go.
On 25 July, however, he stepped down, saying it was "to ensure that anti-national elements do not take advantage of the situation".
Modi's government had reversed course before - most notably when it repealed three farm laws in 2021 after a year of protests. But this climbdown had come remarkably quickly, at the hands of a movement led by people who had been largely unknown only weeks earlier.
Dipke was on stage at the protest site when the news reached him. He dropped to his knees, then sprang up, punched his fist into the air and shouted: "We have done it."
Now that the euphoria of that moment has passed, the CJP is confronting more difficult questions - not least how to hold on to the attention it captured.
Its latest campaign focuses on conditions in government schools in rural India.
"What I'm hoping to accomplish is that children in rural India should at least get a dignified education," said Dipke during a visit to a school in Maharashtra's Hingoli district.
The school had no toilet for female students and expired food packets were being used to prepare lunches. At another, cracks ran through the floors, walls and ceiling.
The campaign has gained some traction, but feels more ad-hoc than a planned national movement, and the CJP still resembles a loose pressure group - something Dipke says is deliberate.
"People have limited politics just to elections and political parties. We want to move beyond that," he said.
"What we are here for is a cultural transformation where people understand their rights, their duties, and how to hold the government accountable no matter which party comes to power."
There are also questions about what the movement chooses to fight for.
Dipke is a Dalit, from a community once considered untouchable and placed at the bottom of India's rigid caste hierarchy. Quotas in jobs and education for lower castes remain deeply polarising.
Over the past decade, India has also seen increasing Islamophobia and deepening religious divides.
Some critics accuse the CJP of avoiding contentious issues affecting Muslims and lower-caste Indians for fear of alienating Hindu supporters. Dipke rejects this.
"I was really happy when, at Jantar Mantar, I used to chant 'Jai Bhim', thousands of other people followed," he said, referring to a slogan associated with Dalit icon BR Ambedkar. "We were also chanting 'Hindu-Muslim politics will not work anymore'."
For now, the bigger test is whether the CJP can turn the extraordinary burst of anger that propelled it into national prominence into something that lasts.
For Dipke, a self-confessed introvert thrust suddenly into public life, the test is also intensely personal.
"I'm the kind of person who would rather spend most of the day alone in my room," he said.
"But now I'm out here among hundreds of people, doing what I must to keep this movement alive - and to sustain the hope they have placed in us."
Additional reporting by Adnan Bhat and Prem Boominathan
